deep.reconstruction:
This page holds no computations or derivations. It is a sequence of methodological and philosophical aphorisms from Hilbert's notebook, continuing the reflections on the previous page (the infinite in mathematics, what mathematics is, refereeing). Item by item:

(1) Problem-solving heuristic. If a problem resists solution, it is often because a nearer, more basic problem has not yet been solved. Illustration: taking off the stockings first and then the boots is impossible; in the reverse order it is easy. In other words, the order of subproblems matters.

(2) Aphorism: a spark of creative power is worth more than whole conflagrations of criticism.

(3) The one mathematically substantive item. 'Seek the invariant of a point set', i.e. find a general law, fixed in advance (definable), that lets one pick a definite point out of any arbitrarily given point set. A first formulation, 'for an arbitrarily given point [set]', is struck out.
- In modern terms Hilbert asks for an explicitly definable choice function F on the nonempty subsets of a space X (e.g. R or R^n), with F(A) in A for every nonempty A.
- Such an F immediately well-orders X, by transfinite recursion: x_alpha = F(X minus {x_beta : beta < alpha}). This step is mine, not on the page.
- The question is therefore tied to Cantor's well-ordering problem for the continuum, which Hilbert raised in Problem 1 of his 1900 Paris address.
- Zermelo (1904) produced such a choice function only by postulating it (the axiom of choice), not by an explicit law.
- Later results show no such definable law exists in ZF (Solovay-type models, Feferman 1965), so the request as stated cannot be met. Read as a demand for a postulated selection 'law', it anticipates Hilbert's own epsilon-operator (epsilon_x A(x)), used from c.1922.

(4) Archimedean axiom. Whether something holds 'with or without Archimedes' means whether it can be proved by a finite number, fixed in advance, of applications of the congruence theorems, or whether infinitesimal (limit) considerations are needed.
- This is the program of Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899): which theorems depend on axiom V.1, as in Dehn's work on Legendre's theorems and Hilbert's theory of area (equidecomposable vs. equicomplementable).
- It also connects to Hilbert's third problem (volume of tetrahedra needs exhaustion).
- Hilbert then applies this to physics. The question must matter for the axioms of physics too. Each application of a congruence theorem might carry a small error, or physical laws might hold exactly only for finite bodies, so that things behave differently in the infinitesimal than in theory. This is a precursor of the sixth problem's demand to axiomatize physics and of his later remarks on the continuum versus physical reality.

(5) The group concept is extremely fundamental but insufficient on its own. Something must be added, e.g. an application to geometry (Klein's Erlangen view) or to number fields (Galois theory).

(6) Methodological advice. Even a superficial classification like fire/water/air/earth is better than none and is a beginning. Collect everything, since every thought and every point eventually finds a use. Seek out analogies and group by methods.
errors: No computational errors are possible since nothing is computed.

Item (3) cannot be fulfilled as an explicit definition. It is consistent with ZF(C) that there is no definable well-ordering, hence no definable choice function, on P(R)\{empty} (Feferman 1965; Solovay 1970). Hilbert's hope for a law 'von vorneherein definirt' is therefore unrealizable, short of postulating a choice operator.

results.what: Request for a law, defined in advance, selecting a definite point from every given point set
results.modern_name: Definable choice function / well-ordering of the continuum; anticipates the epsilon-operator
results.usually_credited_to: Zermelo 1904 (axiom of choice); Cantor (well-ordering problem); Hilbert epsilon-calculus c.1922-1923

results.what: Distinguishing proofs with vs. without the Archimedean axiom (finitely many congruence applications vs. infinitesimal arguments)
results.modern_name: Non-Archimedean geometry; independence of the Archimedean axiom

results.what: The Archimedean question as relevant for the axioms of physics (errors in the infinitesimal, laws exact only for finite bodies)
results.modern_name: Axiomatization of physics (Hilbert's 6th problem); empirical status of the continuum

results.what: Group concept alone insufficient; it needs application (geometry, number fields)

deep.surprise_reason: The page consists of aphorisms. Hilbert's interest in the Archimedean axiom, in axiomatizing physics, and in well-ordering the continuum are all well documented. The explicit formulation of seeking a uniform law that picks a point from every point set is a mildly interesting pre-Zermelo or near-Zermelo precursor of choice functions and of the epsilon-operator, depending on the notebook's date. Given Hilbert's known Problem 1 and his later epsilon-calculus, it is not a major surprise.

checkable.asserts: In R(x) ordered at infinity, x exceeds every integer n, so that field is non-Archimedean. This illustrates the 'ohne Archimedes' setting.
For finite or well-ordered sets a definable selector (min) exists. This is the trivial case of Hilbert's 'selection law'; no analogue is definable for arbitrary subsets of R.
